entries.description: How can client-side end-user interfaces that are physically separated from server-side business logic and data storage be populated and updated with computing results, result sets from searches in data sources, and detailed information about data entities? How can application frontends invoke activities in a backend or upload data to it?

entries.name: Backend Integration
entries.description: How can distributed applications and their parts, which have been built independently and are deployed separately, exchange data and trigger mutual activity while preserving system-internal conceptual integrity without introducing undesired coupling?

entries.name: Public API
entries.description: How can an API be made available to an unlimited and/or unknown number of API clients outside the organization that are globally, nationally, and/or regionally distributed?

entries.name: Community API
entries.description: How can the visibility of and the access to an API be restricted to a closed user group that does not work for a single organizational unit but for multiple legal entities (such as companies, nonprofit/nongovernment organizations, and governments)?

entries.name: Solution-Internal API
entries.description: How can access to and usage of an API be limited to an application, for instance, components in the same or another logical layer and/or physical tier?

entries.name: API Description
entries.description: Which knowledge should be shared between an API provider and its clients? How should this knowledge be documented?

entries.name: Processing Resource
entries.description: How can an API provider allow its clients to trigger an action in it?

entries.name: Information Holder Resource
entries.description: How can domain data be exposed in an API, but its implementation still be hidden? How can an API expose data entities so that API clients can access and/or modify these entities concurrently without compromising data integrity and quality?

entries.name: State Creation Operation
entries.description: How can an API provider allow its clients to report that something has happened that the provider needs to know about, for instance, to trigger instant or later processing?

entries.name: Retrieval Operation
entries.description: How can information available from a remote party (the API provider, that is) be retrieved to satisfy an information need of an end user or to allow further client-side processing?

entries.name: State Transition Operation
entries.description: How can a client initiate a processing action that causes the provider-side application state to change? How can API clients and API providers share the responsibilities required to execute and control business processes and their activities?

entries.name: Computation Function
entries.description: How can a client invoke side-effect-free remote processing on the provider side to have a result calculated from its input?

entries.name: Operational Data Holder
entries.description: How can an API support clients that want to create, read, update, and/or delete instances of domain entities that represent operational data: data that is rather short-lived, changes often during daily business operations, and has many outgoing relations?

entries.name: Master Data Holder
entries.description: How can I design an API that provides access to master data that lives for a long time, does not change frequently, and will be referenced from many clients?

entries.name: Reference Data Holder
entries.description: How should data that is referenced in many places, lives long, and is immutable for clients be treated in API endpoints? How can such reference data be used in requests to and responses from Processing Resources or Information Holder Resources?

entries.name: Link Lookup Resource
entries.description: How can message representations refer to other, possibly many and frequently changing, API endpoints and operations without binding the message recipient to the actual addresses of these endpoints?

entries.name: Data Transfer Resource
entries.description: How can two or more communication participants exchange data without knowing each other, without being available at the same time, and even if the data has already been sent before its recipients became known?

entries.name: Atomic Parameter
entries.description: How can simple, unstructured data (such as a number, a string, a Boolean value, or a block of binary data) be exchanged between API client and API provider?

entries.name: Atomic Parameter List
entries.description: How can multiple related Atomic Parameters be combined in a representation element so that each of them stays simple, but their relatedness becomes explicit in the API Description and the runtime message exchanges?

entries.name: Parameter Tree
entries.description: How can containment relationships be expressed when defining complex representation elements and exchanging such related elements at runtime?

entries.name: Parameter Forest
entries.description: How can multiple Parameter Trees be exposed as request or response payload of an API operation?

entries.name: Data Element
entries.description: How can domain/application-level information be exchanged between API clients and API providers without exposing provider-internal data definitions in the API? How can API client and API provider be decoupled from a data management point of view?

entries.name: Metadata Element
entries.description: How can messages be enriched with additional information so that receivers can interpret the message content correctly, without having to hardcode assumptions about the data semantics?

entries.name: Id Element
entries.description: How can API elements be distinguished from each other at design time and at runtime? When applying domain-driven design, how can elements of the Published Language be identified?

entries.name: Link Element
entries.description: How can API endpoints and operations be referenced in request and response message payloads so that they can be called remotely?

entries.name: API Key
entries.description: How can an API provider identify and authenticate clients and their requests?

entries.name: Error Report
entries.description: How can an API provider inform its clients about communication and processing faults? How can this information be made independent of the underlying communication technologies and platforms (for example, protocol-level headers representing status codes)?

entries.name: Context Representation
entries.description: How can API consumers and providers exchange context information without relying on any particular remoting protocols? How can identity information and quality properties in a request be made visible to related subsequent ones in conversations?

entries.name: Embedded Entity
entries.description: How can one avoid sending multiple messages when their receivers require insights about multiple related information elements?

entries.name: Linked Information Holder
entries.description: How can messages be kept small even when an API deals with multiple information elements that reference each other?

entries.name: Pagination
entries.description: How can an API provider deliver large sequences of structured data without overwhelming clients?

entries.name: Wish List
entries.description: How can an API client inform the API provider at runtime about the data it is interested in?

entries.name: Wish Template
entries.description: How can an API client inform the API provider about nested data that it is interested in? How can such preferences be expressed flexibly and dynamically?

entries.name: Conditional Request
entries.description: How can unnecessary server-side processing and bandwidth usage be avoided when frequently invoking API operations that return rarely changing data?

entries.name: Request Bundle
entries.description: How can the number of requests and responses be reduced to increase communication efficiency?

entries.name: Pricing Plan
entries.description: How can the API provider meter API service consumption and charge for it?

entries.name: Rate Limit
entries.description: How can the API provider prevent API clients from excessive API usage?

entries.name: Service Level Agreement
entries.description: How can an API client learn about the specific quality-of-service characteristics of an API and its endpoint operations? How can these characteristics, and the consequences of not meeting them, be defined and communicated in a measurable way?

entries.name: Version Identifier
entries.description: How can an API provider indicate its current capabilities as well as the existence of possibly incompatible changes to clients in order to prevent malfunctioning of clients due to undiscovered interpretation errors?

entries.name: Semantic Versioning
entries.description: How can stakeholders compare API versions to detect immediately whether they are compatible?

entries.name: Two In Production
entries.description: How can a provider gradually update an API without breaking existing clients but also without having to maintain a large number of API versions in production?

entries.name: Aggressive Obsolescence
entries.description: How can API providers reduce the effort for maintaining an entire API or its parts (such as endpoints, operations, or message representations) with guaranteed service quality levels?

entries.name: Experimental Preview
entries.description: How can providers make the introduction of a new API, or new API version, less risky for their clients and obtain early adopter feedback without having to freeze the API design prematurely?

entries.name: Limited Lifetime Guarantee
entries.description: How can a provider let clients know for how long they can rely on the published version of an API?

entries.name: Eternal Lifetime Guarantee
entries.description: How can a provider support clients that are unable or unwilling to migrate to newer API versions at all?

entries.name: JCA
entries.description: Defines a standard architecture for Jakarta EE application components to connect to Enterprise Information Systems. Formerly Java EE Connector Architecture and J2EE Connector Architecture.

entries.name: Kafka Connect
entries.description: A tool for scalably and reliably streaming data between Apache Kafka and other systems.

entries.name: Apache Arrow (⭐17k)
entries.description: Language-agnostic columnar in-memory format for fast data interchange, including the Arrow IPC format and Flight RPC for moving data between systems.

entries.name: Apache Avro (⭐3.2k)
entries.description: Data serialization system that provides compact, fast, and efficient serialization of structured data. It supports schema evolution, allows for efficient data compression, and is designed to work well with big data processing frameworks.

entries.name: Apache Fory (⭐4.5k)
entries.description: Fast multi-language serialization framework that uses just-in-time compilation and zero-copy techniques, with a cache-friendly row format. Formerly named Apache Fury.

entries.name: Apache Thrift (⭐10k)
entries.description: A serialization and RPC framework originally developed at Facebook that generates cross-language bindings from a single interface definition file.

entries.name: BSON
entries.description: Binary-encoded serialization format for JSON-like documents that is designed to be lightweight and efficient. It supports rich data types and is widely used in NoSQL databases, such as MongoDB.

entries.name: Cap'n Proto (⭐13k)
entries.description: An extremely fast data interchange format and RPC system whose zero-copy encoding doubles as both wire format and in-memory representation.

entries.name: CBOR
entries.description: Concise Binary Object Representation (RFC 8949), a binary data format with a JSON-like data model designed for small message sizes and constrained devices.

entries.name: CSV
entries.description: A simple and widely used data format that stores tabular data in plain text. It is easy to read and write, and can be processed by most programming languages.

entries.name: UN/EDIFACT
entries.description: The United Nations EDI standard for administration, commerce, and transport, dominant outside North America.

entries.name: X12
entries.description: The ANSI-accredited EDI standard widely used in North America for transactions such as orders, invoices, and healthcare claims.

entries.name: FlatBuffers (⭐26k)
entries.description: An efficient cross-platform serialization library from Google that allows direct access to serialized data without parsing or unpacking.

entries.name: NDJSON (⭐843)
entries.description: A standard for delimiting JSON objects in stream protocols. It allows for efficient processing of large JSON datasets and is widely used in big data processing.

entries.name: JSON Lines
entries.description: A text format for storing structured data one record per line.

entries.name: JSON Text Sequence
entries.description: Defined in RFC 7464, describe a specific format for transmitting or storing a sequence of individual JSON texts.

entries.name: JSON
entries.description: A lightweight and easy-to-read data format that is widely used for data exchange. It supports a wide range of data types and is compatible with many programming languages.

entries.name: MessagePack (⭐7.4k)
entries.description: An efficient binary serialization format that lets you exchange data among multiple languages like JSON, but smaller and faster.

entries.name: Protocol Buffers (⭐71k)
entries.description: A language-neutral and platform-neutral serialization mechanism that is designed to be highly efficient and extensible. It supports rich data types and is widely used in distributed systems, such as gRPC and Apache Kafka.

entries.name: XML
entries.description: A flexible and widely used markup language that is used for storing and exchanging structured data. It supports rich data types and is compatible with many programming languages.

entries.name: YAML (⭐499)
entries.description: A human-friendly and easy-to-read data serialization format that is widely used for configuration files and data exchange. It supports rich data types and is compatible with most programming languages.

entries.name: File Transfer
entries.description: Data is exchanged through file exchange between applications.

entries.name: Messaging
entries.description: Applications exchange messages using a messaging infrastructure.

entries.name: Remote Procedure Invocation
entries.description: Applications call functions or procedures on a remote server over a network.

entries.name: Shared Database
entries.description: Multiple applications access and manipulate the same data through a common database.

entries.description: Agent-to-Agent protocol for AI agent interoperability. Enables agents to discover each other via agent cards, exchange messages, and delegate tasks across frameworks and vendors. Created by Google, governed by the Linux Foundation.

entries.name: AMQP 0-9-1
entries.description: A message queuing protocol that enables the exchange of messages between applications or systems. AMQP 0-9-1 provides reliability, security, and flexibility to handle complex messaging scenarios.

entries.name: AMQP 1.0
entries.description: A widely accepted message queuing protocol that provides reliable, interoperable, and efficient messaging between systems. AMQP 1.0 supports a broad range of messaging scenarios and is ideal for complex enterprise-level applications.

entries.name: AS2
entries.description: A protocol for secure and reliable transport of EDI and other business documents over HTTP/S, using S/MIME for signing and encryption.

entries.name: AS4
entries.description: An OASIS profile of ebMS 3.0 for secure, web-services-based B2B document exchange, widely mandated in e-government networks such as Peppol.

entries.name: CoAP
entries.description: A specialized application protocol designed for constrained devices in the Internet of Things (IoT) ecosystem. CoAP offers a lightweight, low-overhead communication mechanism to support resource-constrained devices.

entries.name: gRPC
entries.description: A high-performance, open-source RPC framework that uses HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers, with support for streaming, pluggable load balancing, and authentication.

entries.name: HTTP
entries.description: A widely used protocol that facilitates communication between web servers and clients. HTTP enables the transfer of data over the internet, making it possible for web applications to function seamlessly.

entries.name: JSON-RPC
entries.description: A simple and lightweight remote procedure call protocol that enables communication between systems using JSON data. JSON-RPC offers stateless communication and is suitable for resource-constrained devices.

entries.name: MCP
entries.description: Model Context Protocol for AI agent-to-tool connectivity. Standardizes how AI agents discover and interact with external tools, data sources, and APIs. Created by Anthropic, governed by the Linux Foundation.

entries.name: MQTT
entries.description: A lightweight and efficient publish-subscribe protocol that supports messaging between devices. MQTT enables low-overhead communication and is ideal for IoT and mobile applications.

entries.name: OpenMessaging (⭐287)
entries.description: A cloud native, vendor-neutral open specification for distributed messaging.

entries.name: Server-Sent Events
entries.description: A WHATWG standard for pushing text-based event streams from servers to clients over plain HTTP.

entries.name: SOAP
entries.description: A messaging protocol that uses XML to enable communication between systems. SOAP supports a wide range of messaging scenarios, including distributed computing and enterprise applications.

entries.name: STOMP
entries.description: A messaging protocol that offers simple, text-oriented communication between systems. STOMP is ideal for low-latency, high-performance messaging scenarios.

entries.name: WebSocket
entries.description: A protocol providing full-duplex, bidirectional communication channels over a single TCP connection, ideal for real-time applications.

entries.name: FHIR
entries.description: HL7's Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources standard, defining RESTful APIs and resource formats for exchanging healthcare data.

entries.name: JDBC
entries.description: A Java-based API that provides universal data access to relational databases. JDBC offers a consistent and efficient way to access and manipulate data, making it a popular choice among developers.

entries.name: JMS
entries.description: A messaging API that enables Java applications to send and receive messages. JMS supports reliable messaging and is widely used in enterprise-level applications.

entries.name: ODBC
entries.description: A widely accepted API that provides a standardized way to access data from various database management systems. ODBC offers a consistent interface to access data, making it easy to develop database applications.

entries.name: OData
entries.description: An open protocol that enables the creation and consumption of queryable and interoperable REST APIs. OData simplifies the development of REST APIs and offers a standardized way to access data.

entries.name: Open Banking
entries.description: UK standard defining secure APIs that enable banks to share account and payment data with authorized third-party providers.

entries.name: JSON Schema (⭐5.1k)
entries.description: A powerful tool for validating the structure of JSON data. JSON Schema enables developers to ensure that JSON data conforms to a specific structure, making it easier to process and manipulate.

entries.name: Schematron
entries.description: A rule-based validation language that enables developers to define and validate business rules, data reporting, quality control, and other validation scenarios. Schematron offers a flexible way to validate XML documents.

entries.name: XML Schema
entries.description: A schema language that offers facilities for describing the structure and constraining the contents of XML documents. XML Schema enables developers to ensure that XML data conforms to a specific structure, making it easier to process and manipulate.
